body.x: AES Tech (CEO Jaehong Jeffrey Chun) participated in the ‘Global Media Meetup’ held on July 30. Organizers arranged this meetup to inform overseas media about participating companies’ products and technologies in advance for global markets while expanding business opportunities. AES Tech joined this meetup as a company submitting its modular hydrogen supply system ‘ammoNOVA Ultra’—which extracts hydrogen on-site from liquid ammonia—for the CES 2027 Innovation Awards, with CEO Jaehong Jeffrey Chun delivering the presentation on this day.

A surge in power demand triggered by AI lies in the background. The International Energy Agency (IEA) projects global data center electricity consumption to more than double from approximately 415 TWh in 2024 to around 945 TWh by 2030. The core challenge is that power grid connections and new power generation facilities struggle to keep pace with the construction speed of data centers. Consequently, a trend to place dedicated power generation sources near data centers emerged, and gas turbines capable of fast startup, output adjustment, and short installation periods surfaced as a realistic alternative. However, because burning natural gas leaves carbon emissions, gradually increasing hydrogen co-firing ratios requires hydrogen supply systems as well as generators to move in sync with gas turbine operational changes.

body.cap: Illustration depicting a 4-unit parallel configuration of AES Tech’s ammonia-based on-site hydrogen production module ‘ammoNOVA Ultra’ | Image provided by AES Tech

body.x: Conventional hydrogen supply methods face clear limits here. Transporting central-produced hydrogen via tube trailers continuously incurs compression, storage, transportation, and safety management costs, making it difficult to supply large-volume flow rates consistently. Thermal crackers using ammonia as a raw material must maintain high temperatures continuously, creating thermal inertia in responding to startups and load fluctuations. The exact point AES Tech targets is “producing hydrogen on-site immediately as much as needed.”

ammoNOVA Ultra is a 20-foot standard module that electrochemically extracts hydrogen from anhydrous liquid ammonia. Because it controls reactions by supplying electric current to electrochemical stacks instead of decomposing ammonia with heat, hydrogen production volume connects directly with stack current, allowing it to follow second- and minute-by-minute gas turbine load fluctuations. Design goals presented by the company include daily hydrogen production of approximately 240 pounds, operation at 10 to 100 percent output, load fluctuation tracking of 40 percentage points within 1 minute, 99.999 percent hydrogen purity, and ammonia slip below 50 ppmv. Company officials explain that these represent design targets for commercial modules, distinguished from current achieved values.

body.cap: AES Tech CEO Jaehong Jeffrey Chun (left) during an interview with Ubergizmo Editor-in-Chief Hubert Nguyen | Photo by AVING News

body.x: Core differentiators reside in stack structure and emission characteristics. AES Tech’s ‘SCC’ structure aims to integrate serration-based sealing, rear-side cooling channels on separator plates, uniform clamping via bending and leaf springs, and shunt current suppression channels into a single stack, eliminating separate cooling cells and reducing stack length by over 30 percent. Furthermore, because oxygen does not participate in the electrolysis process, it avoids the nitrogen oxide (NOx) emission issues that thermochemical methods face when decomposing ammonia at high temperatures. Unhydrogenated ammonia remaining after reactions is recirculated in a closed loop rather than discarded, through which the company targets an energy efficiency of over 90 percent.

The system also took scalability into account. Because large gas turbines require more hydrogen than a single module provides, instead of indefinitely scaling up equipment, standard 20-foot modules connect in parallel via a common header to expand incrementally from 1 to 4 units, operating remaining modules even during maintenance of specific units. Combined with this is the control platform ‘ACE-UP’, which collects sensor data in real time to compare against normal operation models and detect abnormal signs early. The company explains this not as complete autonomous operation, but as a control platform stage assisting anomaly detection and operational judgment.

body.cap: Ubergizmo Editor-in-Chief Hubert Nguyen (left) and AES Tech CEO Jaehong Jeffrey Chun take a commemorative photo after concluding the Global Media Meetup. | Photo by AVING News

body.x: In the US, cases of large AI and cloud corporations alongside power generation companies introducing gas turbines directly at data center sites rather than waiting for grid connections are increasing, and AES Tech targets fuel supply for hydrogen co-firing in this trend. Domestically, the company executes empirical projects with government support. Currently commercializing a compact product half the size of a 20-foot unit to supply development-demand companies, the company will unveil its full commercial model, ammoNOVA Ultra, for the first time at CES 2027.

Jaehong Jeffrey Chun, CEO of AES Tech, explained, “Even if gas turbines offer power flexibility for AI, burning natural gas leaves carbon emissions at the combustion stage.” He added, “The goal is to produce hydrogen on-site from ammonia as much as needed, gradually raising the co-firing ratio.” He continued, saying, “However, clean characteristics are not guaranteed automatically, and environmental benefits materialize when electricity used and ammonia production pathways are low-carbon.”
